title: U.S. Senate · South Carolina

context.text: This election fills the Class II Senate seat formerly held by Lindsey Graham (R), who won renomination in the June 9, 2026 Republican primary and died on July 11, 2026. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham's sister, Darline Graham, to the seat on July 13, 2026. A special Republican primary (August 11) and runoff (August 25) were held to select the party's replacement nominee; Darline Graham won that runoff and appears on the November 3 general-election ballot.
Annie Andrews won the Democratic primary on June 9, 2026 with 61.5% of the vote, defeating Brandon Brown and Kyle Freeman.
Kasie Whitener won the Libertarian Party's nominating convention on April 11, 2026.

candidates.name: Darline Graham
candidates.ballotNote: Won the special Republican primary runoff (Aug. 25, 2026) to become the general-election nominee after Lindsey Graham's death

summary.text: Darline Graham is the Republican U.S. Senator from South Carolina, appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster on July 13, 2026 after the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham. Before the Senate she worked in state vocational-rehabilitation and disability-services agencies, and from 2019 headed the South Carolina Commission for the Blind. She won the Republican special primary runoff on August 25, 2026 and is running to complete the term.

background.text: Born in Central, South Carolina, on June 12, 1964. Her parents operated a restaurant and bar; her mother died when she was 11 and her father about 15 months later, after which she lived with an aunt and uncle in Seneca, with her brother Lindsey as her legal guardian.

Earned a bachelor's degree in sociology from the College of Charleston (1989) and a master's degree in rehabilitation counseling from South Carolina State University (2009); she is also a Certified Public Manager.

In 2008 she joined the South Carolina Vocational Rehabilitation Department, where she helped coordinate a remote-work program for adults with severe disabilities and by 2015 was public information director.

In 2019 she became commissioner and agency head of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, which administers vocational rehabilitation, independent living and blindness-prevention programs. She also served on the South Carolina State Workforce Development Board and was elected president of the National Council of State Agencies for the Blind, with a term set to begin in January 2027.

Before her appointment she had not held elected office; she appeared in a 2002 television ad for her brother's Senate campaign and took part in his later campaigns, including introducing him at his 2016 presidential campaign launch.

Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her on July 13, 2026 to fill the vacancy created by Lindsey Graham's death, and she was sworn in July 14. She is the first woman to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate and the first senator to succeed a sibling.

In the 2026 special Republican primary on August 11 she placed first with 32.8% and advanced to a runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman, which she won on August 25 with 52.6% of the vote (180,231 to 162,497 per Ballotpedia).

Her committee assignments, per Wikipedia, are Appropriations, Budget, Environment and Public Works, and Judiciary. On July 16, 2026 she introduced the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which passed both chambers and was signed into law in September.
Lives in Lexington, South Carolina, and has two daughters, according to Wikipedia.

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website, issue statements, or Candidate Connection survey response found for Darline Graham as of research date; she has held office only since July 2026. Background is from Ballotpedia's biographical summary.

candidates.name: Annie Andrews
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 9, 2026 Democratic primary with 61.5% of the vote

summary.text: Annie Andrews is a pediatrician and the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. She worked as a pediatric hospitalist at the Medical University of South Carolina and was the 2022 Democratic nominee in South Carolina's 1st Congressional District. She describes herself as a pediatrician and a mom, not a politician, and says she takes no corporate PAC money.

background.text: Born in 1981 in Paducah, Kentucky, and raised in Indianapolis, Indiana, according to Wikipedia.
Earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Dayton, an M.D. from the University of Cincinnati and a master's degree in clinical research from the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC).

Completed a pediatrics residency in Cincinnati, then moved to South Carolina's Lowcountry in 2009. She worked about 14 years at MUSC Children's Hospital in Charleston as a pediatric hospitalist and was a professor of pediatrics at MUSC.
According to her campaign website, she spent nearly two decades in children's hospitals before turning to advocacy and policy work on school safety, health-care access and abortion rights.
Became politically active after the 2018 Parkland shooting, joining Moms Demand Action and doing clinical research on firearm injury prevention in children.

Ran for Congress in South Carolina's 1st District in 2022, her first campaign; she was the Democratic nominee and lost to Rep. Nancy Mace, 56.5% to 42.5%. She resigned from MUSC in 2023 and started a PAC, Their Future. Our Vote.

Announced her U.S. Senate candidacy on May 29, 2025 and won the June 9, 2026 Democratic primary with 61.5% of the vote. She was running against Lindsey Graham until his death on July 11, 2026, and now faces Darline Graham.
Lives in Charleston with her three children, who attend public schools, according to her campaign website.

candidates.name: Mark Hackett

summary.text: Mark Hackett is the Constitution Party candidate for U.S. Senate in South Carolina. He has run for U.S. House as the party's nominee in 2020 and 2024 and is making his first statewide run in 2026. Little biographical information about him is publicly available.

background.text: Ran as the Constitution Party candidate for South Carolina's 6th Congressional District in 2020, receiving 0.9% (2,646 votes) in the general election won by James Clyburn.

Won the Constitution Party convention vote (8 to 5) on April 13, 2024 and ran in South Carolina's 4th Congressional District, receiving 2.8% (9,779 votes) in the general election won by William Timmons.
Is on the November 3, 2026 ballot for U.S. Senate as the Constitution Party candidate.

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website or public issue statements found in a 2026-10-19 search.

candidates.name: Kasie Whitener
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Libertarian Party of South Carolina's nominating convention on April 11, 2026
candidates.currentRole: Assistant professor; former Libertarian Party of South Carolina Chair

summary.text: Kasie Whitener is a former chair of the Libertarian Party of South Carolina and the party's 2026 U.S. Senate nominee. She was born in Florence, South Carolina, holds a Ph.D., and has worked as an assistant professor.

background.text: Born in Florence, South Carolina, and graduated from Herndon High School.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Clemson University (1999), a graduate degree from Winthrop University (2004) and a Ph.D. from Capella University (2014).
Her career experience includes working as an assistant professor.
Served as chair of the Libertarian Party of South Carolina.
Defeated Jason Brenkus at the Libertarian Party convention on April 11, 2026 to become the party's U.S. Senate nominee.

priorities.text: Passing a balanced budget amendment and reducing the national debt.
Taking on the two-party system and making constituents, not party operatives, the priority.
Getting government out of the way so people can prosper.

positions.summary: Wrote in a December 2025 blog post that government should not be in the health insurance business.
positions.quote: Government should not be in the health insurance business.

positions.summary: Wrote in March 2026 that only Congress can declare war and that the President had committed two acts of war without authorization.
positions.quote: Only Congress can declare war and the President has now committed two acts of war without authorization.

positions.summary: Wrote in an April 2026 blog post opposing state millionaire's taxes and billionaire tax proposals, saying the real problem is government overspending.
positions.quote: Except these taxes aren’t about generating revenue for the state. They’re about punishing the wealthy for being wealthy.

positions.summary: Wrote in August 2025 that tariffs make it difficult for companies with foreign roots in South Carolina to get the parts they need.
positions.quote: Tariffs hurt those companies by making it difficult for them to get the parts they need to build their products.

researchNotes: Basic-tier research. Darline Graham was appointed to this seat in July 2026 after Lindsey Graham's death; her federal key-vote and FEC data (if added later by script) will reflect only her short tenure. This slate and the Graham appointment/death were independently confirmed against Wikipedia, CBS News, and the official senate.gov senator roster (which lists 'Graham, Darline' for South Carolina, Class II), since the sole cited source was Ballotpedia. Andrews's summary originally called her a 'Charleston pediatrician' citing only her Ballotpedia page, which does not state her profession; corrected to cite her campaign website, which confirms she is a pediatrician (no independent confirmation that she practices in Charleston specifically, so that detail was dropped). Five independent candidates (Jack Ellison, Cindy Glaser, Paul Sedletsky, Edward Strunge, Reece Wright-McDonald) were removed on 2026-10-19: Ballotpedia's race page (s1) lists them under 'Withdrawn or disqualified candidates', and SC Daily Gazette (s18, Oct. 12, 2026) describes the ballot as Andrews, Graham, Whitener and Hackett only; a Democratic write-in candidate (Catherine Fleming Bruce) is not included per the write-in exclusion in the research standard's ballot scope. Biography pass: Ballotpedia's 2026 race page and candidate pages list Jack Ellison, Cindy Glaser, Don Louis, Paul Sedletsky, Edward Strunge and Reece Wright-McDonald under 'Withdrawn or disqualified candidates', so the independents' ballot status should be rechecked; no biographical information was found for them or for Mark Hackett beyond his earlier campaigns.
